messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Maid
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 51

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Three years ago, Arjun was deep in the west wing of a client’s historic townhouse. He had positioned a stepladder to reach the top of a tall linen closet. The floor was newly waxed, slick under his work boots. When he shifted his weight to grab a heavy cast-iron ironing board leaning against the wall, the ladder’s rubber feet caught on a hairline crack in the tile. It buckled. The board slipped from his grip, pivoted on the edge of the step, and fell backward. It struck the homeowner’s nephew, who had just walked into the hall, squarely across the temple. There was no slow-motion unraveling, just two sharp frames that lock in his mind: the sudden tilt of the ladder beneath his boots, and the sickening arc of the iron board descending toward the man’s face. The event happened because of the way he had acted; he was certain of that. The aftermath did not bring a steady stream of recollection but a series of frozen moments that would drop into his awareness without warning. Sometimes it was the smell of lemon floor polish on a Tuesday morning; other times, it was the particular squeak of a metal hinge or the sight of a heavy object balanced on a high surface. In those moments, the hallway would warp, his palms would sweat, and the two pictures would snap back into place so completely that his breath would catch. When the image returned, a hot, sharp fury would coil in his chest. It was not directed at the man who had been hurt. The anger was aimed at himself, at the way his hands had moved, at the carelessness that felt so alien to the man who had always prided himself on quiet competence. What frightened him most was how instantly the room would fill with the memory, leaving no space for anything else. His job as a residential cleaner had required steady hands and a meticulous eye for three decades. After the incident, Arjun found himself avoiding the very tasks that once came naturally. He began taking the long route to the east staircase of each new house, refusing to use stepladders, and he started cleaning each room in a slow, almost halting pace. He quit the agency that employed him at the historic properties, taking lower-paying jobs in single-story homes where the ceiling felt closer and the corners offered fewer places for things to fall. The change accumulated quietly. He stopped answering calls from old friends who asked if he wanted to help them move or do minor renovations. He began spending his days in his small, dim apartment in Queens, drawn to the silence because movement reminded him of the shift in weight, the crack in the tile, the sudden arc. Over time, Arjun had come to believe he was fundamentally reckless, a trait he had spent his life fighting against. At the same time, nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore. His days and nights ran side by side without crossing, each occupying its own space in his mind. He stopped volunteering at the community center he had attended for years, stopped tending to the small balcony garden that had always given him structure. The work that once grounded him now felt like an exercise in waiting. He could not reconcile the man he was with the man who had caused harm, and the disconnect made his days feel weightless. He carried both convictions forward, parallel and unyielding. Arjun finally walked into the clinic after a regular shift at a corporate office. He was wiping down a supply closet shelf when a heavy binder slipped from a neighbor’s grip and landed on the rubber floor with a dull thud. The sound had paralyzed him against the wall, his heart hammering against his ribs, the two frames flashing behind his eyes until he had to leave before the shift ended. He had spent his life believing he could manage a space with careful work, but he no longer trusted his own hands or his own judgment. He came to the appointment hoping for something he could not name—perhaps a way to quiet the fury that rose in him when he remembered, or a way to stop feeling like a stranger in his own routine. He did not know if he would ever feel purposeful again, but he knew he could no longer carry the weight of the mistake alone.
